days.title: Discerning False Prophets
days.summary: The New Testament warns that false prophets will arise with convincing signs and speeches. A true prophet is recognized by character, faithfulness to God’s will and the fulfillment of the messages.
body: The New Testament warns that spiritual deception will mark the last days: false prophets will arise, able to perform signs and persuade even the sincere (Matt. 24:11; Matt. 24:23-25; 2 Pet. 2:1-3). Not everyone who speaks in Jesus’ name represents His message, and counterfeits can be very convincing.

That is why the biblical counsel is not to accept everything, but to test it (1 Thess. 5:19-22; 1 John 4:1-6). Jesus taught that a tree is known by its fruit (Matt. 7:15-20): a true prophet is not recognized only by words or manifestations, but by character, agreement with God’s will and the fulfillment of the messages.

Christians are called to stand firm, clothed in the armor of God — truth, faith and watchfulness (Eph. 6:10-18). And even before supernatural forces, there is one certainty: nothing can separate God’s people from His love (Rom. 8:38, 39).

days.title: The Supreme Prophet
days.summary: Moses announced a prophet like himself, and the New Testament shows that it was Jesus. The same Word who created all things became flesh — and He is the source of all prophetic light.
body: Moses predicted: “The Lord thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet […] like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken” (Deut. 18:15). Peter confirmed in Jerusalem that this prophecy pointed to Jesus (Acts 3:22). Jesus is the Supreme Prophet, the One to whom all the Old Testament prophets pointed (Mark 8:27-29; Luke 24:13-35).

The description of the Word in John 1:1-5 does not fit any ordinary human being: “All things were made by him” (John 1:3). The Creator of everything became flesh (John 1:14). In every “And God said” of Genesis 1 we hear the voice of Jesus, and the One who said “Let there be light” (Gen. 1:3) is “the light of men” (John 1:4).

The prophetic words are like a light that shines in a dark place (2 Pet. 1:19), and they will keep shining until Jesus, “the bright and morning star” (Rev. 22:16), establishes His eternal kingdom. Until then, through His life, death and resurrection, He offers eternal life to everyone — the decision is whether to accept that gift.

What changes when you read Genesis 1 knowing it is Jesus’ voice saying “Let there be light”?
What “dark” areas of your life need the light of the prophetic word?

days.title: Jesus and His Word at the Center
days.summary: Ellen White’s ministry revolved around two things: leading people to Jesus and pointing them to the Bible. She saw her writings as a “lesser light” that leads to the “greater light.”
body: God called prophets to lead people to know Him and to have a relationship with Him — and that was the center of Ellen White’s ministry. The five-volume Conflict of the Ages series begins and ends with the words “God is love.” In Steps to Christ she wrote that our growth in grace depends on “communion with Him, daily, hourly.”

While writing The Desire of Ages in the 1890s, she noted in her diary: “I forget to breathe as I ought. I cannot bear the intensity of feeling that comes over me as I think of what Christ has suffered” (Selected Messages, book 3).

Her second focus was the Bible. She called her writings a “lesser light,” meant to lead people to the “greater light” — the Scriptures — and said: “I recommend to you, dear reader, the Word of God as the rule of your faith and practice.” For her, those with the gift of prophecy must teach what Christ had taught (The Desire of Ages).

days.title: Many Voices
days.summary: We are shaped by what we see and hear most — often more by the algorithm than by Scripture. Hearing God’s voice requires a willingness to silence our own wishes.
body: Social media, opinions and trends try to tell us who we should be and how to live. We have never had so much information, and yet many people feel confused. Little by little, we realize we are being shaped more by the algorithm than by the Scriptures (Heb. 3:15).

While still young, Samuel was sleeping in the temple when he heard someone call him. He thought it was Eli; only later did he understand it was God (1 Sam. 3:1-10). Before becoming a prophet, he had to learn that hearing God’s voice requires willingness. We often look only for messages that confirm what we already want to hear.

During World War II, pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer chose to remain faithful to the gospel while many religious leaders kept silent before Nazism — and it cost him his freedom and his life. Among so many voices, God keeps speaking through the Bible; the challenge is to quiet our own hearts to hear Him.
reflect: Which voices most influence the way I think and make decisions today?
How can I tell, in practice, God’s voice from the other voices around me?
In what ways have I let what I consume every day shape my choices more than the Lord’s voice through His Word?

days.title: General and Special Revelation
days.summary: Nature reveals God’s power and love, but it also shows evil. Only special revelation — Jesus and the Bible — interprets that message correctly, and the Holy Spirit guided the prophets through the whole process.
body: God often speaks without words: general revelation, visible in nature, shows His power and His care (Rom. 1:19, 20). But the natural world also displays the presence of evil (Gen. 3:14-19; Matt. 13:24-30). That ambiguous message is only understood correctly through special revelation — Jesus, the Word made flesh, and the Bible, the written Word that testifies of Him (John 5:39).

The Scriptures record creation, the fall, the plan of redemption and the final restoration of the earth (2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:20, 21). Prophetic inspiration is the work of the Holy Spirit: He guided the prophets not only to receive the messages, but also to pass them on clearly.

God used many methods: visions and dreams (Num. 12:6; Isa. 6:1, 8), eyewitnesses (1 John 1:1-3), historical research guided by the Spirit (Luke 1:1-3) and impressions on the mind (2 Pet. 1:21). And the prophets delivered the message orally, in writing (John 20:30, 31) or even through symbolic acts (Ezek. 4:1-8).

Why do we need special revelation to understand the world we live in?

days.title: Receiving and Passing On
days.summary: In Revelation, the message went from the Father to Jesus, to the angel, to John and to the readers. Jesus told John to write so that nothing would be lost, and each author’s style does not lessen inspiration.
body: Exiled on Patmos, John received messages for the seven churches of Asia and for Christians of every age (Rev. 1:1-3; Rev. 1:9-11). The chain of revelation followed this order: God the Father; Jesus Christ; the angel; John; and finally the readers and hearers — a classic example of how God uses prophets to speak to humanity.

If John had not written, the message could have been lost or distorted. That is why Jesus commanded: “Write the things which thou hast seen” (Rev. 1:19). Writing gives permanence to the spoken word. The books of the Bible reflect each writer’s style, but that does not lessen the validity of the messages: there are no “degrees” of inspiration.

The writers sometimes recorded messages they had preached, as Moses did in Deuteronomy. They even quoted uninspired sources (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) and words of Satan (Gen. 3:1-5; Matt. 4:1-11), and recorded good and bad examples (1 Cor. 10:1-11). The Bible was not written in perfect language, but it carries an infallible message.

days.title: Symbols, Parables and Enacted Messages
days.summary: Daniel and Revelation speak through symbols, Jesus taught with metaphors and parables, and prophets like Ezekiel and Hosea acted out messages. The shock had a purpose: to wake up a people who rejected the warnings.
body: Revelation is full of symbols — beasts and horns (Rev. 13:1), stars and lampstands (Rev. 1:20), symbolic women (Rev. 12:1; Rev. 17:3) — in the same style as Daniel, who represents kingdoms with a statue (Dan. 2:31-45), animals and horns (Dan. 7; 8). It seems hard on a quick reading, but the dedicated student discovers that the Bible itself gives the interpretation. Even the sacrificial system was a symbol of Christ’s sacrifice and His heavenly priesthood (Heb. 8:1-6).

Jesus taught with metaphors: the Bread of Life (John 6:35), the Light of the world (John 8:12) and the True Vine (John 15:1-8). He also explained His kingdom with parables, like that of the sower (Matt. 13:1-9; Matt. 13:18-23).

Ezekiel made a model of Jerusalem and lay before it 390 days on his left side, for Israel, and 40 days on his right side, for Judah (Ezek. 4:1-8). Hosea married Gomer, a prostitute, symbolizing Israel’s unfaithfulness (Hos. 1:2-9). These scenes were meant to shock: when the warnings were rejected (2 Chron. 36:15-21), this was the last act of mercy to lead the people to repentance.

days.title: How God Communicates
days.summary: The Bible was written by real people, guided by the Holy Spirit. Some did research, others saw and touched, some only preached — because the Word finds the form the human heart needs.
body: The Bible was written by real people, guided by the Holy Spirit: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2 Tim. 3:16). Luke consulted witnesses, John said he had seen and touched what he described, and Paul even quoted pagan poets — inspiration does not require ignorance of the world, but discernment.

Not every prophet wrote: Noah preached for decades without leaving a book, and Ezekiel acted out prophecies with bricks and iron pans. God speaks through His servants, the prophets (Jer. 1:9; Amos 3:7; Heb. 1:1, 2; 2 Pet. 1:19-21).

And He insists. Out of compassion, He sent messengers again and again, rising up early, but the people mocked them (2 Chron. 36:15, 16; Jer. 7:23-26). God’s Word always finds the form the human heart needs to receive what it does not yet want to hear.

days.title: Oral Messages
days.summary: Before any written record, God spoke audibly and clearly. Noah, Elijah, John the Baptist and Jesus Himself delivered messages orally — with the same authority as those who wrote.
body: Before any text, God’s messages were heard. He spoke with Adam and Eve before and after the fall (Gen. 2:16, 17; Gen. 3:9-19), and His voice was heard clearly at Sinai (Exod. 20:1-20), at Jesus’ baptism and at the transfiguration (Matt. 3:17; Matt. 17:5). We may misunderstand others, but when God speaks, there is no mistake on His side.

Isaiah (Isa. 8:1; Isa. 8:11), Jeremiah (Jer. 1:4; Jer. 1:9) and Ezekiel (Ezek. 3:16) said they heard God’s voice. Denying this is questioning the prophets’ honesty. Noah, “a preacher of righteousness” (2 Pet. 2:5), wrote nothing in the Bible, but his preaching was no less inspired. The same is true of Nathan, Elijah, Elisha and John the Baptist.

And Jesus? The only record of Him writing anything is when He “wrote on the ground” with His finger (John 8:6). Even so, He taught “as one having authority” (Matt. 7:29), and His hearers admitted: “Never man spake like this man” (John 7:46). His words had no less authority because He did not write a book.

days.title: Revelation and Inspiration
days.summary: Ellen White received the same kind of inspiration as the Bible prophets, but she never placed her writings on the level of the Bible. She understood that God inspires people, not words — and that not everything she wrote was inspired.
body: Adventists believe that Ellen White was inspired and that her life and ministry meet the criteria of a true prophet. She received the same kind of inspiration as the Bible prophets, but she never considered her writings on the level of the Scriptures — and neither do we. For her, the Bible is the infallible, authoritative revelation.

She understood inspiration as an interaction between the divine and the human: “It is not the words of the Bible that are inspired, but the men that were inspired” (Selected Messages, book 1). God communicates the thought; the prophet expresses it in his or her own words. The Bible, she wrote, presents a union of the divine and the human.

She also made it clear that not everything was inspired: “There are times when common things must be stated, common thoughts must occupy the mind, common letters must be written.” That distinction matters when reading personal letters and diaries — and it helps us avoid extremes and read her writings wisely.

days.title: Signs of the Holy Spirit in My Life
days.summary: We do not see the Holy Spirit, but we notice His signs in attitudes and choices, like a fragrance in the air. Having the Spirit is not being perfect; it is being transformed.
body: A new fragrance in the house needs no explanation: you do not see it, but you notice that something has changed. The Holy Spirit’s work is similar — we do not see Him, but we notice His presence in a person’s attitudes, words and choices.

The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force or a religious emotion: He is a divine Person, sent to convict, comfort, guide and transform. Paul says He produces fruit: “love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance” (Gal. 5:22, 23) — a character shaped day after day.

Many look for extraordinary signs, but the most important ones are small changes: wanting to ask for forgiveness, holding back a harsh reply, doing the right thing when you do not feel like it, seeking the Word, being bothered by sin. Having the Spirit is not being perfect, but being in a process of transformation.

days.title: Literary Genres and Styles
days.summary: The prophets communicated the message in three ways: speaking, writing and acting it out. The writings were given to lead to salvation, and no literary style has more authority than another.
body: The Bible shows three main ways of communicating God’s message: orally, in writing and through symbolic acts. The oldest was direct communication — an audible voice, dreams or angels. Only in Moses’ time do we find the first command to record in “a book” what God had spoken (Exod. 17:14).

The prophetic writings were given to lead the people to salvation, not to satisfy curiosity about the future (Jer. 36:3). Whenever the messengers were impressed to write, the Holy Spirit enabled them — in the desert, fleeing from Saul or exiled in Babylon.

There are very different styles: texts that resemble a diary (Num. 33:1-49), metaphors and hyperboles, and apocalyptic writings in Daniel, Zechariah and Revelation, with strong symbolism and cosmic themes. Even so, there is no difference in authority between one style and another.

days.title: Literary Assistants
days.summary: Jeremiah dictated his messages to Baruch, and Paul used Tertius to write Romans. The secretaries were faithful to the meaning but could influence the vocabulary — what is inspired is the prophet’s thought.
body: When the officials in Jerusalem heard Baruch read Jeremiah’s scroll, they asked how it had been written. He explained: “He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book” (Jer. 36:18). Jeremiah could have written alone, but he trusted a secretary.

In the New Testament, Tertius says: “I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord” (Rom. 16:22). He was Paul’s amanuensis, that is, the assistant who recorded his words. Many scholars explain in this way the differences in style between Paul’s letters and between 1 and 2 Peter: if even Paul, fluent in Greek, used secretaries, Peter, who spoke Aramaic, probably did too.

The secretaries were faithful to the thought and meaning the prophet wanted to convey, but the vocabulary and sentence structure could reflect their skill. In the end, what is inspired is the prophet’s thought, not necessarily every word chosen to express it.
reflect: Who helped make it possible for you to read the Bible in your own language?
What can we do today to help more people know the prophets’ message?
Why does knowing that the prophets used secretaries not lessen our confidence in the Bible?

days.title: Literary Sources
days.summary: The prophets also used outside sources: Solomon collected proverbs, Ezra and Nehemiah copied letters and lists, Luke did research and Jude quoted a non-biblical book. The Holy Spirit guided even that selection.
body: Solomon did not compose all the proverbs he recorded: he “gave good heed, and sought out, and set in order many proverbs” and “sought to find out acceptable words” (Eccles. 12:9, 10). The description of the virtuous woman in Proverbs 31 is attributed to the mother of King Lemuel (Prov. 31:1), and there are signs of the influence of Egyptian literature in parts of the book.

Ezra included copies of royal letters and decrees (Ezra 4–7), and Nehemiah incorporated genealogical lists he found (Neh. 7:5-72). In the New Testament, Luke carefully researched and gathered eyewitness accounts (Luke 1:1-4).

Other authors quoted works outside the Bible: Paul quoted Greek philosophers without naming them (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12), and Jude seems to quote the so-called “First Book of Enoch,” a Jewish work that was not written by Enoch. The Holy Spirit not only gave visions and dreams, but also guided the messengers in choosing what to use.

days.title: A Divine and Human Treasure
days.summary: The Bible was born from the meeting between the Holy Spirit and imperfect people. God preferred shepherds, fishermen and kings to angels — the same logic as the incarnation: a Word both divine and human.
body: The Bible did not fall from heaven as a document written by angels in heavenly language. It was born from the meeting between the Holy Spirit and imperfect human beings: Solomon selected proverbs, the historians quoted royal archives and Paul quoted Greek poets to reach those who did not know the Scriptures.

God could have used angels as scribes, but He preferred shepherds, fishermen, kings and former persecutors — a treasure in earthen vessels (2 Cor. 4:7). It was not carelessness: it is the logic of the incarnation. The Word who became flesh (John 1:14) shows the same principle as all of Scripture: a Word perfectly divine and genuinely human.

Jesus often asked “Have ye not read?” (Matt. 12:3-5; Matt. 19:4; Mark 12:10), showing the importance of reading and studying when doubts arise. And everything written in the past was written for our learning and hope (Rom. 15:4) — with a blessing for those who read and keep it (Rev. 1:3).

When a doubt comes up, is your first reaction to search the Word or the internet?
With the logic of the incarnation in mind, how do you read the “human” parts of the Bible?

days.title: Treasure in Earthen Vessels
days.summary: The prophets used imperfect human language to communicate God’s perfect thoughts. A few difficult passages do not affect the essence of the message, and we can trust the accuracy of the revealed truths.
body: Prophetic messages combine divine action and human participation: God speaks, and the prophets use imperfect human language to communicate His perfect thoughts. Paul sums it up: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2 Cor. 4:7).

The messengers were not protected from personal failings — think of Moses, Elijah, David, Jonah and Peter — and their writings also reflect limits of understanding and language. Just as Jesus had a divine and a human nature, the Bible also has both dimensions: “The truths revealed are all ‘given by inspiration of God’; yet they are expressed in the words of men” (Testimonies for the Church, vol. 5).

The Holy Spirit did not prevent some texts from seeming hard to harmonize today. They are few, and it is not wise to let them become a stumbling block: we submit to the Word as we understand it and trust God in what we do not yet understand. These points do not affect the essence of the message, and God’s truths are revealed accurately.

days.title: The Writings of Ellen White
days.summary: Weakened after her accident, Ellen White heard the angel say: “Write.” Like the Bible prophets, she relied on secretaries and used other sources, without ever trying to seem more than she was.
body: Ellen White also received the task of writing what was revealed to her. Weakened by the accident that nearly cost her life, she thought she could not do it. But the angel insisted: “Write the things I give you.” She took a small writing board and found that she could trace the words with ease (General Conference Bulletin, May 31, 1909).

Like the Bible writers, she relied on literary assistants. Her secretaries did editorial work: they helped express the message clearly, without adding their own thoughts — they were not “ghostwriters” or co-authors. She also quoted and adapted other sources, and she recommended the same books she used, with no intention of deceiving anyone.

Her human traits were not erased by the call: she grew and matured throughout her life. And she corrected those who thought every word she spoke came from heaven: common letters had to be written, and such words and information were “not given under special inspiration” (Selected Messages, book 3). She never tried to seem more than she was.

days.title: Between Trends and Eternal Truths
days.summary: We have never had so much access to the Bible and so little knowledge of it. The greatest danger may not be rejecting it, but getting used to it.
body: We are the generation with the most access to the Bible in history — and one of those that knows it least deeply. Many young people know more trends, memes and viral songs than promises from Scripture. Perhaps the greatest danger is not rejecting the Bible, but getting used to it: reading without noticing, opening the text without letting it open the heart.

The prophets did not treat the message as something ordinary. Jeremiah said: “Thy words were found, and I did eat them” (Jer. 15:16). Daniel studied the earlier writings, and people risked their lives to preserve these texts — while we often leave the Bible closed out of distraction.

A strong generation is not born only from exciting services, but from young people who learn to love the Word in secret. Study context, history and prophecy, but remember: knowledge without transformation produces only religious information.
reflect: How much time do I spend feeding my mind with online content compared to the time I spend letting God’s Word transform my heart?
How does studying inspiration, human imperfections, literary genres and the prophets’ assistants strengthen my confidence in the Bible and in Ellen White’s ministry?

days.title: Angry at God’s Message
days.summary: When personal “truth” clashes with God’s Truth, many rebel. Joshua and Caleb, and later Jeremiah, stood firm even in the face of violent opposition.
body: Today many are encouraged to treat their own “truth” — experiences, opinions, convictions — as absolute. The problem arises when it clashes with the Truth revealed in Jesus and in His Word. The prophets brought messages the people did not want to hear, and so many were rejected, persecuted and killed (Heb. 11:32-38).

When the spies returned from Canaan talking about giants and fortified cities, the people panicked, wanted to go back to Egypt and turned against Moses and Aaron (Num. 13:31; Num. 14:1-4). Joshua and Caleb stayed faithful and pleaded: “Only rebel not ye against the Lord” (Num. 14:9). The reaction was so hostile that they were almost killed.

The same conflict marked Jeremiah’s ministry. God told him to speak everything he was commanded, without fear (Jer. 1:17), and promised to make him firm as “an iron pillar” (Jer. 1:18). Even with intense resistance, he remained faithful, sustained by divine strength.

days.title: Destroying the Message
days.summary: Even with Judah’s sins, God insisted in love: Jeremiah bought a field as a sign of hope and wrote a final appeal. King Jehoiakim cut up the scroll and burned it — but the message did not disappear.
body: Idolatry, child sacrifice, adultery and oppression were common in Jeremiah’s day, and the prophet’s appeals were ignored. Even so, God’s messages remained redemptive. He told Jeremiah to buy a field and keep the deed: “Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land” (Jer. 32:15) — a sign that the people would return from exile.

Out of love, God had a final appeal written down. Baruch wrote and read the message in Jerusalem; the officials, alarmed, advised Baruch and Jeremiah to hide (Jer. 36:19). King Jehoiakim heard only the beginning, became furious, cut the scroll into pieces and threw it into the fire (Jer. 36:20-23).

Sometimes we think that if we ignore or destroy God’s message, it will disappear. But indifference does not erase the Word; it only makes the consequences worse. The prophecy about Jehoiakim’s end (Jer. 36:30, 31) is a warning: we ignore divine warnings at our own risk.

days.title: A History of Resistance
days.summary: Jeremiah prophesied through five reigns. Zedekiah did not humble himself before the one who spoke “from the mouth of the Lord,” and the rejection of the prophets led Judah into exile — a story that grieved Jesus.
body: Jeremiah’s ministry spanned the reigns of Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah. When Zedekiah took the throne at 21 (2 Chron. 36:11), Nebuchadnezzar had already plundered Jerusalem. The Bible says he “did that which was evil” and “humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the Lord” (2 Chron. 36:12).

Jeremiah was a sinful man like anyone else, but he represented the Lord. For centuries, God sent messengers to His people (Jer. 25:4; Matt. 11:13; Luke 11:49), because He is “not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2 Pet. 3:9). The history of Israel and Judah is the account of God’s tireless effort to reach an unfaithful people.

In the end, the grace Jeremiah offered was met with mockery and contempt. The rejection of the prophets led to exile in Babylon (2 Chron. 36:15-21) and grieved Jesus: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee” (Matt. 23:37).

days.title: The Price of Being a Prophet
days.summary: Israel’s rebellions were recorded as a warning for us. We may not openly mock the messengers, but we can reject the message by accepting only what pleases us.
body: Israel’s history in the wilderness was recorded as a warning: Paul says these accounts were written so that we would not repeat the same mistakes (1 Cor. 10:6-11). And God promises strength to overcome temptation (1 Cor. 10:12, 13).

Today we may not openly mock God’s messengers, but we can reject the message in subtle ways: ignoring biblical counsel, relativizing the truth or accepting only what pleases us. Rejecting the divine message is, in the end, rejecting God Himself.

Jeremiah felt the weight of this. He wept for the people (Jer. 9:1; Jer. 13:17), even cursed the day he was born (Jer. 20:14-18) and was threatened with death (Jer. 26:8-11; Jer. 38:4). Even so, he could not keep quiet: God’s word was like a fire shut up in his bones (Jer. 20:9).

days.title: For Our Admonition
days.summary: The sad stories of the Old Testament were preserved so that we can learn from them. We are not doomed to repeat the mistakes of the past if we take God’s warnings seriously.
body: The Old Testament accounts, as sad as they are, were preserved so that we would learn what happens when we rebel against God. “These things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted” (1 Cor. 10:6). The past helps us understand the present and the future.

Paul says these things “are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come” (1 Cor. 10:11), linking ancient Israel to the church today (Gal. 6:14-16). We are not doomed to repeat the mistakes of earlier generations if we take the warnings seriously. “Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12) — and God gives strength to overcome (1 Cor. 10:13).

If we are willing to listen and obey, we will be safe and prosper (2 Chron. 20:20). God does not waste words: they stand forever (Isa. 40:8). And if that was true in Paul’s day, it is even more true for us.

days.title: Dreams and Visions
days.summary: Ellen White received hundreds of visions, some accompanied by supernatural signs and witnessed by skeptics. As in Bible times, some accepted and others rejected — and she asked for patience and love toward those who doubted.
body: Ellen White received hundreds of visions and dreams, lasting from minutes to hours and sometimes witnessed by large groups, including skeptics. In 1868, her husband, James White, described it: she was completely unaware of her surroundings, did not breathe, her muscles were rigid, yet her gestures were “free and graceful” and her eyes remained open. No one controlled when the visions came.

As in Bible times, some accepted the messages and others rejected them. She wrote that she had not chosen this unpleasant work for herself and that she would warn, counsel, reprove and encourage, whether people listened or not (Testimonies for the Church, vol. 4).

Many rejected her messages out of unbelief or personal disputes, not for theological reasons. She treated skeptics courteously and asked that they be treated with “patience and brotherly love” (vol. 1). For her, the confirmation of the gift was in the messages themselves, and God gives sufficient evidence for faith to rest on the side of truth.

days.title: When Truth Confronts the Heart
days.summary: Our culture says to follow your own “truth.” When it clashes with God’s truth, we have to choose — and the prophets faced resistance precisely because they called for change.
body: Our culture encourages everyone to follow their own “truth.” When it clashes with God’s truth, we have to choose between His guidance and our own way. The prophets faced resistance precisely because they called people to repentance and change.

Israel let the fear of Canaan turn into unbelief and rebellion, while Joshua and Caleb trusted the promises. Jeremiah also had to stand firm in the face of criticism. And Jehoiakim burned the scroll — showing that rejecting the Word does not remove its consequences.
The Bible stories were preserved as a warning (1 Cor. 10:11). God wants us to learn from the mistakes of the past and to cultivate a life of trust, humility and obedience.
reflect: How can I tell my feelings apart from God’s truth?
What fears today might weaken my trust in God?
In what ways might I be ignoring the Lord’s voice without realizing it?
